lead: An iOS app moves from source text to a compiled bundle, an installed copy, a running process, and a paused process under the debugger. Xcode organises this work with a project, target, scheme, bundle identifier, Info.plist and asset catalogue. You edit, build, install, run and debug. Build errors appear before installation; crashes appear only when a line executes. The debugger lets you stop at a breakpoint, inspect variables with LLDB, walk the view hierarchy, and read Apple's documentation with Option-click. Only a few universities teach these tools in depth, so exams often test the order of steps and the meaning of a crash message.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.3, because there must be a class or struct worth running.

sections.h3: The Xcode project and what a build does

blocks.text: An Xcode project is the folder that holds source files, settings and resources. A target is one product built from that project, usually the app. A target also lists the files and build settings used for that product. A scheme names the targets to build, the build configuration for each action, and the executable/launch settings; the run destination is chosen separately in the toolbar. The bundle identifier is the app's unique reverse-domain name, such as com.example.fares. Info.plist stores app metadata and permission text. The asset catalogue stores images and colours. The daily loop is edit, build, install, run, debug.

A build compiles every Swift file and links the results with frameworks into an .app bundle. A compile error stops the build. A warning does not stop it. A runtime crash happens only after install, when a line executes. The figure shows this order. Only a few universities teach these tools in depth; exams often ask the order.

Choose the simulator for fast testing on the Mac, or a connected device for real camera, sensors and performance. Press Run; Xcode builds, installs, launches and attaches the debugger. A breakpoint is a line marker that pauses execution there. The debug area shows variables and the call stack. Step over runs the current line and stops on the next; step into enters a called function. Simulator builds are faster; device builds need code signing.

The LLDB console accepts commands. po fares prints an object or value. A runtime crash opens the same debug area at the crashing line. The view hierarchy debugger shows every view's frame and order, useful when a control is invisible or misplaced. Option-click any type or method in the editor to open Apple's documentation. The loop is edit, build, install, run, debug, then fix and rebuild. Use breakpoints sparingly; each pause lets you inspect, not guess.

Read a crash message in two parts. The first line names the error, such as Fatal error: Index out of range. The stack trace lists the functions active at the crash, with your code usually near the top. A breakpoint set on the suspect line pauses before the bad access, so you can inspect values. Compile errors and runtime crashes need different fixes. A compile error means the compiler rejected the text; the app never installed. A runtime crash means the binary ran and a condition failed. Warnings may hint at the cause but do not stop the build.

The worked example separates the two. For an index crash, check the array count and the range operator. Use the half-open range, or loop over the elements directly. The debugger shows the count and the elements, so check both before editing. Fix the smallest line, rebuild, and rerun the same path. Do not change unrelated code during a debug session.

figure.caption: The debugger prints fares as 92, 158 and 65 at indices 0, 1 and 2; the closed range 0...fares.count also asks for index 3, so the app stops there with Fatal error: Index out of range. The fix is 0..<fares.count, and because the app had already built and installed, this is a runtime crash, not a build error.

spec.title: fares = [92, 158, 65], count 3
spec.aria: One row named fares holds the values 92, 158 and 65 at indices 0, 1 and 2, all marked valid, and a fourth box at index 3 marked as the first bad index that the closed range 0...fares.count reaches, which stops the running app with an index out of range crash.

examples.question: An iOS app stores let fares = [92, 158, 65] and prints each fare with for i in 0...fares.count { print(fares[i]) }. The app is built, installed and run. Explain what the debugger shows when the loop crashes, give the valid index range, the first bad index, and the smallest code fix. State whether this is a build error or a runtime crash.
steps: The valid indices are 0, 1 and 2. The last valid index is 2.
The closed range 0...fares.count includes 3, so the loop reaches fares[3].
The debugger pauses on that line with Fatal error: Index out of range.
po fares prints [92, 158, 65], confirming the count is 3.
Fix: use the half-open range up to fares.count, or write for fare in fares.
examples.answer: The array has 3 elements, valid indices are 0 to 2, the first bad index is 3, and the crash is a runtime crash, not a build error.
examples.check:
fares = [92, 158, 65]
n = len(fares)
print(n)
print(n - 1)
print(n)

traps: Calling a red runtime crash a compile error: build errors stop before install; index crashes happen only when the line runs.
Using a closed range over an array count, which visits one index past the end.
Thinking the simulator and a device behave identically; sensors and performance differ.
Confusing step over with step into; step into enters a function.

quiz.a: The targets to build, the build configuration for each action, and the executable/launch settings; the run destination is chosen separately in the toolbar.

quiz.q: Why does a compile error stop before install?
quiz.a: The compiler rejects source text, so no .app bundle is produced.

quiz.q: Fares has 4 elements. What is the first bad index in the closed range over fares.count?
A crash appears only after tapping a button. Is it a build error? Explain.
quiz.a: No; the code compiled and ran, so it is a runtime crash on that path.

quiz.q: Which LLDB command prints a value?

quiz.a: Runs the current line and stops on the next, without entering calls.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, Xcode builds run on continuous integration servers, and automated UI tests replace some manual runs. Instruments profiles memory and time; the view hierarchy debugger is a daily tool for layout bugs. Search for Xcode schemes, LLDB, and Instruments.
